{"id": "68:1/q15", "question": "What does the opening oath swear by and how is it joined?", "turns_on": "Whether Nūn is itself sworn by, whether the first wāw is oath or conjunction, and how coordination transfers oath force.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q15/p1", "position": "The wāw before the Pen begins or continues an oath, and the wāw before mā coordinates another oath object.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās says the first wāw coordinates with Nūn rather than beginning a new oath; Elmalılı says this depends on whether Nūn itself is an oath. Samarāʾī argues coordinated objects inherit the oath force, citing 79:1–5."}, {"id": "68:1/q15/p2", "position": "An omitted 'Lord of' yields an oath by the Lord of Nūn and Pen.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Jishumī transmit this ellipsis."}, {"id": "68:1/q15/p3", "position": "It swears by the pen's writers and their written lines, through metonymy.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī and Rāzī make al-qalam stand for its users, making the plural pronoun intelligible."}, {"id": "68:1/q15/p4", "position": "The whole oath honors the familiar letter, writing and the proof against the pagans.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers this, taking the wāw as an oath of exaltation; Iṣlāḥī says the oath substantiates the opening claims."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q16", "question": "What is the answer to the oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q16/p1", "position": "The negative assurance in 68:2 that Muhammad is not mad, with further assurance of reward.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Qushayrī, Jishumī and al-Samīn identify the next verse; Muqātil supplies the accusers Abū Jahl, ʿUtba and Shayba. Ibn ʿĀshūr points also to 68:51 and 81:22; Iṣlāḥī says the oath supports three opening claims."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q17", "question": "How does this opening answer its opponents?", "turns_on": "The nature of the opponents' charge and whether the pen points to scripture itself or to writing more generally.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q17/p1", "position": "It refutes the charge of madness and vindicates Muhammad's revelation, character and reward.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Abū Jahl, ʿUtba and Shayba; al-Qalam compares the Prophet with corrupt Quraysh leadership. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ emphasizes the pagans' allegation of ancient tales; the closing verses return to the vindication."}, {"id": "68:1/q17/p2", "position": "The Qurʾān and its writing provide the evidence for prophethood.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī argues the recorded Qurʾān's elevated discourse and earlier scriptures testify; Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the pen and writing to the Book that caused the taunts."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q18", "question": "How does the opening connect to other verses and sūras?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison uses muṣḥaf adjacency, revelation chronology, shared words or thematic parallels.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q18/p1", "position": "It follows al-Mulk's warning and final image of water, moving from divine power to knowledge and guidance.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Abū Ḥayyān connect denials and threats; Biqāʿī makes life-giving water in 67:30 a transition to reviving spirits with knowledge. Iṣlāḥī sees a pair with a sterner second member; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects that chronological revelation order does not support an original sequential context."}, {"id": "68:1/q18/p2", "position": "It recalls the first revelation's teaching by the pen in 96:1–5.", "reasons": "Asad, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connect Read, letters, writing and prophethood; al-Qalam's early position strengthens the link."}, {"id": "68:1/q18/p3", "position": "It alludes ahead to Jonah as companion of the fish at 68:48.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī calls the surviving fish sense of Nūn a sūra-name allusion; Elmalılı accepts an allusion while rejecting it as primary."}, {"id": "68:1/q18/p4", "position": "It pairs with Qāf as knowledge and power.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī contrasts hidden fish or nūn knowledge with visible encircling Mount Qāf and kings' bodily power; both initials encompass the public Qurʾānic section."}, {"id": "68:1/q18/p5", "position": "Its short oath suits a shorter denial than al-Ṭūr's long oath.", "reasons": "Samarāʾī compares 52:1–6 with this verse and relates the extra denial of soothsaying in al-Ṭūr to the extended oath."}, {"id": "68:1/q18/p6", "position": "The closure circles back to the opening vindication.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ sees 68:51 and the closing support for the Prophet returning to the opening denial of madness."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q19", "question": "What is reported about this sūra's name, place, sequence and verses?", "turns_on": "Transmission on chronology and count, and whether portions are distinguished from the sūra as a whole.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q19/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, has fifty-two verses, and is named Nūn, al-Qalam or Nūn wa-l-Qalam.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Bayḍāwī and Suyūṭī give the count; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes names in tafsirs, ḥadīth collections and a fifth-century Kufic codex. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ excepts 17–33 and 48–50 from the early Meccan material."}, {"id": "68:1/q19/p2", "position": "It was among the earliest revelations, often ranked second after al-ʿAlaq.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī instead places al-Muddaththir before it and al-Ḍuḥā after; Jābir ibn Zayd ranks it before al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir, while Ibn ʿĀshūr favors ʿĀʾisha's al-Muddaththir report. Asad, Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Study Quran call this the earliest disjoint-letter opening."}, {"id": "68:1/q19/p3", "position": "A report promises reciters reward like people of excellent character.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits a report from Ubayy without a grading."}, {"id": "68:1/q19/p4", "position": "Most of it concerns al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr report this; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports the attribution. Separate ʿAlī reports assign the unguided accusers and guided status to him."}, {"id": "68:1/q19/p5", "position": "Counting the isolated letter as a verse depends on regional convention.", "reasons": "Zarkashī says Basrans count no disconnected opening as verses, Kufans count some, and Wāḥidī singles out Ṭā Hā."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q20", "question": "What inward account does the verse give of existence and knowledge?", "turns_on": "The correspondence assigned to Nūn, Pen and inscription, and whether the lesson concerns cosmology, knowledge or spiritual conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q20/p1", "position": "Nūn is Universal Soul, Pen is Universal Intellect, and their inscription produces forms and states of beings.", "reasons": "Qāshānī says intermediary intellects and holy spirits figuratively write, while God is the real writer; the oath honors the beginnings of divine ordination."}, {"id": "68:1/q20/p2", "position": "Nūn is undifferentiated essential knowledge, Pen is detailed named knowledge, and writing unfolds the Book of Existence.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya's seed and tree analogy and the hidden Book's letters, words, verses and sūras; divine knowledge is identical with Essence in his account."}, {"id": "68:1/q20/p3", "position": "Nūn is pre-eternity and primordial light specially bestowed on Muhammad.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar says Muhammad's great character at 68:4 is the pre-eternal light singled out for him."}, {"id": "68:1/q20/p4", "position": "The fish's burden teaches reward for bearing the divine trust.", "reasons": "Bursevī says the fish was sworn by and spared slaughter; likewise the believer who bears trust is spared separation."}, {"id": "68:1/q20/p5", "position": "Witnessing divine gentleness yields independence from creatures and praise in both gift and deprivation.", "reasons": "Qushayrī develops this ethical inward lesson."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q21", "question": "How is the written sign نٓ represented and inflected?", "turns_on": "Whether the written single letter is a paused name or an independent symbol whose possible case is inferred.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q21/p1", "position": "The single written sign stands for the pronounced letter name nūn, which is read in a paused, uninflected form.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr notes the exceptional use of one sign for the three-letter name, as in other openings; Zajjāj says sukūn only fits a letter name. Naḥḥās reports al-Farrāʾ's comparison with ثم or the plural نون; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that a noun would be written in full."}, {"id": "68:1/q21/p2", "position": "Independent opening letters can bear several possible syntactic cases without a fixed place.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says an independent comprehensive letter can be parsed as nominative, accusative or genitive because no relation forces one case."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q22", "question": "What claims are made about the Qurʾān's alphabetic composition?", "turns_on": "Whether composition from ordinary letters is used to argue miraculous expression or the Qurʾān's createdness.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q22/p1", "position": "The fourteen distinct opening letters are half the Arabic alphabet.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ counts fourteen of the alphabet's letters across the openings."}, {"id": "68:1/q22/p2", "position": "Because the Qurʾān is made of the familiar letters, the openings expose the audience's inability to match it.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects the counted letter set to the challenge of inimitability."}, {"id": "68:1/q22/p3", "position": "The letters show that the Qurʾān is composed of letters and is created.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports Abū Bakr al-Zubayrī's theological inference without choosing it."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q23", "question": "How are competing reports and explanations of نٓ assessed?", "turns_on": "The authority of transmitted reports and the grammatical or lexical evidence for each gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q23/p1", "position": "Only the alphabet-letter account is reliable among the proposed glosses.", "reasons": "Al-Baḥr rejects the other senses; Ālūsī questions how this squares with al-Ḥākim's authentication and al-Ḍiyāʾ's collection and points

to contradictory Ibn ʿAbbās reports."}, {"id": "68:1/q23/p2", "position": "The inkwell gloss is linguistically uncertain.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports Zamakhsharī's uncertainty over whether the term is linguistic or revealed, common or proper, and diptote; Ālūsī disputes its poetic witness."}, {"id": "68:1/q23/p3", "position": "A criticism of al-Zamakhsharī's treatment is recorded without its details.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls an argument here erroneous but the note does not reproduce the argument."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q24", "question": "What parallels are proposed between alphabetic openings?", "turns_on": "Whether a letter's fit is local to its sūra or part of a broader contextual pattern.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q24/p1", "position": "Each opening letter is said to fit its own sūra's wording or theme.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports that Qāf's many qāf words span revelation, creation and resurrection; substituting qāf for nūn would spoil the fit."}, {"id": "68:1/q24/p2", "position": "A contextual survey should test one rationale for all letter-opened sūras.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says her proposed pattern also fits al-Rūm's final defense against deniers and appeal for patience (30:58–60)."}, {"id": "68:1/q24/p3", "position": "Al-ʿAnkabūt, al-Rūm and Nūn are exceptions to the usual opening-letter pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī refers the reason to Asrār al-Tanzīl."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q25", "question": "How is lengthening handled before the final nūn's assimilation?", "turns_on": "Whether assimilation changes the duration of the prolonged sound before the still consonant.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q25/p1", "position": "The madd has a required minimum before the still consonant, though specialists name its degree differently.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports full saturation, enabling the madd, and a rank below hamza lengthening as descriptions."}, {"id": "68:1/q25/p2", "position": "Assimilation takes longer madd than clear pronunciation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥātim, al-Dānī and others reason that the sound continues through assimilation, comparing dābba and muḥyāy."}, {"id": "68:1/q25/p3", "position": "Clear pronunciation takes longer madd than assimilation.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿIzz says the assimilated consonant gains strength from the next consonant and its vowel."}, {"id": "68:1/q25/p4", "position": "The two take equal madd.", "reasons": "Most readers say both contain adjacent still consonants, the operative cause."}, {"id": "68:1/q25/p5", "position": "The same clear versus assimilated choice occurs in other initials.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī cites Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm in 26:1 and 28:1, where Ḥamza and Abū Jaʿfar pronounce the nūn clearly."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q26", "question": "Are terms such as inkpot and pen exclusively Arabic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q26/p1", "position": "Shared words belong to every language that uses them ordinarily; no language gains proven priority without decisive evidence.", "reasons": "Abū Maysara says the Qurʾān has words from every language. Ṭabarī cites inkwell, pen, paper, dirham and dinar as shared usage; he prefers describing them as Arabic-Ajamic or Ethiopic-Arabic and rejects exclusive origin claims without proof."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q27", "question": "What examples show the effects of writing and decree?", "turns_on": "The different examples of beneficent decree, harmful human inscription, inferred divine knowledge and practical power.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q27/p1", "position": "Written decree can console one who grieves.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī reports Ibn al-Zayyāt comforting a caliph by invoking divine favor and what was already written on the Tablet."}, {"id": "68:1/q27/p2", "position": "A written boycott documents a harmful human deed.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī recalls Quraysh's pact against Banū Hāshim and allies as an example of the writings included under the phrase."}, {"id": "68:1/q27/p3", "position": "The pen's knowledge and its Lord are inferred from its rational writers.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu recounts Elmalılı's sequence from writing to reason, the First Pen and the Lord of worlds."}, {"id": "68:1/q27/p4", "position": "Sword strength and pen knowledge govern worldly order.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī connects sword with Qāf and al-Ḥadīd's strength, and the pen with this sūra's disclosure of knowledge."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q28", "question": "How is saṭr related to other written accounts?", "turns_on": "The lexical relation of writing lines to the disputed noun for earlier accounts.", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q28/p1", "position": "The verb means to write or inscribe.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and al-Suyūṭī transmit Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatāda's straightforward gloss."}, {"id": "68:1/q28/p2", "position": "Asāṭīr are written accounts of earlier people, not necessarily disordered false tales.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba rejects Abū ʿUbayda's singular usṭūra or isṭāra and his gloss of baseless tales without order."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q29", "question": "What observations about Qurʾānic script accompany the pen theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q29/p1", "position": "Some spelling choices depart from ordinary script conventions.", "reasons": "Zarkashī notes the wāw form of ولما in Hūd and Yūsuf versus fāʾ elsewhere and the separation of أن لا in ten places including al-Qalam; al-Marrākushī argues letter forms vary with meanings."}]}
{"id": "68:1/q30", "question": "What otherwise associated report concerns the later warning against bad character?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:1/q30/p1", "position": "A report excludes a hoarding miser, coarse brute and base gluttonous oppressor from Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits it from the Prophet and illustrates the traits by 70:15–16 and 3:159; the note concerns the later description in this sūra."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q01", "question": "What is the Lord's favor in this verse?", "turns_on": "The sources identify the favor as mercy, protection, prophethood, broader personal gifts, or inward knowledge; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ also distinguishes the form niʿma from naʿīm.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q01/p1", "position": "God's mercy.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Māwardī gloss niʿma as mercy; al-Wāḥidī transmits Muqātil's gloss alongside the Meccan accusation."}, {"id": "68:2/q01/p2", "position": "The gift of prophethood, often together with faith.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās specify faith and prophethood; al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī and others say prophethood makes madness untenable. Bayḍāwī adds sound judgment; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers prophethood as the decisive proof over general virtues."}, {"id": "68:2/q01/p3", "position": "The Lord's protection.", "reasons": "Reported as an alternative gloss by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī."}, {"id": "68:2/q01/p4", "position": "God's gifts of reason, character, wisdom, courage, and fitness for the mission.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās points to intellect and understanding; al-Ṭabrisī names full intellect, prophethood and wisdom. Al-Rāzī, al-Muntakhab, al-Biqāʿī, al-Elmalılı and the reported alternative in al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī add eloquence, conduct, freedom from defects, nurturing, the Qur'an and worldly and afterlife felicity. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds prophethood more decisive."}, {"id": "68:2/q01/p5", "position": "Insight into what the Soul and Intellect inscribe and into hidden destinies.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī interprets the favor as unveiled insight into destiny and realities; Najm al-Dīn says the Prophet is not veiled from the eternal past or future."}, {"id": "68:2/q01/p6", "position": "In Qur'anic usage, niʿma denotes worldly blessings, while naʿīm denotes afterlife bliss.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says her survey in al-Takāthur, citing 102:8, found this distinction between the two forms."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q02", "question": "How does 'by your Lord's favor' fit the sentence?", "turns_on": "The disagreement is over what governs the first bāʾ phrase and whether a circumstantial attachment would restrict the denial to the Prophet's favored state.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q02/p1", "position": "It gives the cause or means of the negation: madness is absent through God's favor.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq attach it to the negation; the comparison is attributing intelligence or freedom from poverty to God's blessing. Al-Ṭabrisī estimates an omitted removal of madness; Ibn al-Ḥājib attaches it to the verbal sense of mā, favored by Ibn Hishām, though Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that grammarians generally do not let a particle govern an adverbial. Naṣir al-Dīn calls the bāʾ causal. Al-Samīn attaches it to the conveyed sentence meaning."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial phrase attached to the negated predicate majnūn or its pronoun.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says the extra predicate bāʾ does not block majnūn from governing an earlier qualifier, just as an affirmed predicate can; the sense is 'not mad while favored.' Al-Qurṭubī gives it an accusative circumstantial role. Al-Nasafī refers to an omitted expression with accusative position governed by majnūn; Elmalılı also reports a stable state from anta. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that the scope of negation could imply only madness-with-favor is denied; Naṣir al-Dīn and al-Ālūsī raise the same restriction, and Bayḍāwī questions its sense. Al-Khafājī illustrates the scope with a line about a campfire at night."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p3", "position": "It is a circumstantial phrase governed by the sense of negation, qualifying the Prophet while favored.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī treats the meaning of negation as its governor; al-Bursawī describes an omitted state qualifying the pronoun in majnūn. Al-Ālūsī says the first bāʾ marks association and the second is emphatic; Naṣir al-Dīn prefers the unrestricted denial while the Prophet has sound judgment, prophecy and courage."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p4", "position": "It is a parenthetical praise, 'praise be to God,

Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers the ordinary Arabic aside and rejects a merely semantic alternative."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p5", "position": "An omitted conjunction gives 'you are not mad, and the favor belongs to your Lord.'", "reasons": "Compared to 'Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You.' Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī cite Labīd and al-Nābigha for understood words in coordinated phrases; al-Samīn says Labīd's line illustrates meaning rather than a syntactic parse. Abū Ḥayyān describes this as a semantic gloss, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects it as no parsing."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p6", "position": "The bāʾ introduces an intervening oath by the Lord's favor.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī observe that bāʾ as well as wāw marks oaths. The Shaykh, Abū Ḥayyān and Najm al-Dīn prefer this to a restricted circumstantial denial; the oath's answer may be unstated or inferred from the surrounding clause."}, {"id": "68:2/q02/p7", "position": "A parenthetical clause has the bāʾ attached to an omitted predicate: 'that is by your Lord's favor.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this because it follows Arabic usage, citing 11:41 and al-Faḍl ibn ʿAbbās al-Lāhibī's verse using bi-niʿmat Allāh."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q03", "question": "What does 'your Lord' add to the wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q03/p1", "position": "It honors the Prophet and promises God's continued favor and elevation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says calling God his Lord signals that God will complete His favor and raise him to unmatched heights."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q04", "question": "How are mā, anta, and bi-majnūn parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q04/p1", "position": "Mā has anta as its subject and majnūn as its predicate; the predicate bāʾ affects its form.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Nasafī give subject and predicate; the grammarians cited by Bint al-Shāṭiʾ call bāʾ extra, assigning surface genitive to majnūn while its underlying predicate position remains nominative or accusative in their differing descriptions."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q05", "question": "What force does the bāʾ before majnūn carry?", "turns_on": "Whether the grammatical label 'extra' adequately describes the bāʾ's necessary semantic effect, and whether that effect is emphasis or categorical denial.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q05/p1", "position": "It intensifies the negation.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī say the added bāʾ reinforces denial. Ibn Hishām counts such added bāʾs as meaningful emphasis. Ibn ʿĀshūr counts it with the oath and nominal negative clause as three reinforcements against 68:51. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts this bāʾ with the emphatic lām of the disbelievers' assertion at the sūra's end."}, {"id": "68:2/q05/p2", "position": "It makes the denial categorical; the particle has a necessary semantic role.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects 'extra' as implying dispensability. Her survey finds bāʾ on explicit single-word predicates of mā and laysa, usually a categorical denial; in negative questions it yields insistent affirmation. She cites many Qur'anic examples, including 27:81, 8:51, 2:74, 75:40 and 39:36. She says grammarians assign the bāʾ to wording rather than meaning."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q06", "question": "What does majnūn mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "The lexical sense is shared; the derivational issue concerns attested Arabic usage versus a regular formation.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q06/p1", "position": "A person deprived of reason, whose mind is covered.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās relates the root to night, fetus, grave, and shield covering something; a line by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa uses majnī for a shield. Al-Jishumī says junūn is lost reason from concealment; al-Bursawī calls it a barrier between soul and intellect and allows jinn striking, heart injury, or separation of soul and intellect."}, {"id": "68:2/q06/p2", "position": "Its attested form majnūn follows Arabic usage although regular derivation would give majn.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports the idiom ajanna fa-huwa majnūn and contrasts the regular majn; al-Mubarrad favors a regular derivation from janna."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q07", "question": "What does the denial of madness establish about the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The notes move from a direct denial of insanity to what that denial proves about character, mission, or success.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q07/p1", "position": "The charge is false, and God has given the Prophet reason, virtue, and sound character.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls him the wisest of his time; al-Rāzī points to eloquence, intellect, conduct, virtue and lack of defects, and says 38:86 rules out affected character because pretense eventually fails. Al-Biqāʿī recalls forty years of trusted conduct and the Qur'an's coherence, citing 17:88 and 4:82. Al-Muntakhab says favor removes a blameworthy trait and gives praiseworthy traits; the Study Quran links 68:4's character to the opposite of possession."}, {"id": "68:2/q07/p2", "position": "The denial vindicates his messengership and the divine guidance he brings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the polytheists called him mad to avoid admitting his mission, so denying madness restores that claim. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says prophethood itself excludes the mental disorder alleged to invalidate guidance. {"id": "68:2/q08", "question": "What accusation or event prompted this assurance?", "turns_on": "The reports vary between a general Quraysh charge, an account after Ḥirāʾ, named opponents, and an insult against ʿAlī; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects restricting general wording by reported occasions.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q08/p1", "position": "Meccan or Quraysh opponents called Muhammad mad, sometimes alleging demonic possession.", "reasons": "15:6 preserves their taunt that the recipient of the Reminder is mad. {"id": "68:2/q14", "question": "What is reported about when this verse was revealed?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ over which passage was first: the opening of al-ʿAlaq or 87:1.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q14/p1", "position": "It belongs to the sūra's first five verses among the earliest revelation after Ḥirāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives Ibn ʿAbbās's Ḥirāʾ narrative with 96:1, then says God swore against Quraysh's charge in the first five verses. {"id": "68:2/q15", "question": "How does the assurance affect the Prophet and later believers?", "turns_on": "The reported extension to later followers broadens the immediate reassurance to Muhammad.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q15/p1", "position": "It consoles and steadies the Prophet against hostile accusations.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says God removes distress; al-Biqāʿī says the great oath comforts him and the enhanced denial honors him. {"id": "68:2/q16", "question": "What rhetorical pattern do these verse endings illustrate?", "turns_on": "The rhetorical works use the passage to exemplify different sound and composition figures.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q16/p1", "position": "Balanced ornament, including tarsīʿ with tajnīs, related figures, and close sounding endings.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī lists Qur'anic parallels including 68:3, 7:201, 100:7, 52:1–2 and 79:3–4, then Imruʾ al-Qays, Abū Nuwās and Ibn al-Rūmī for tarsīʿ. He cites al-Khansāʾ for muḍāraʿa, sayings attributed to al-Manṣūr, ʿUmar ibn Dharr, Bashshār and Arabs for takāfuʾ near antithesis, and Imruʾ al-Qays for taʿaṭṭuf. Al-Burhān says Qur'anic endings use identical or phonetically close letters, citing al-Qamar and al-Fātiḥa."}, {"id": "68:2/q16/p2", "position": "The adjacent endings exemplify iltizām, committing to extra letters before the rhyme.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān defines luzūm mā lā yalzam as an unforced commitment to one or more letters before the rhyme and says 68:2–3 commit to two. Nearby it reports Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ's twin-meter verse device and other theorists' extension of tashrīʿ to prose in which a complete clause gains a second rhyming clause."}]}
{"id": "68:2/q17", "question": "What does this verse illustrate about reading Qur'anic passages together?", "turns_on": "How far textual parallels may be treated as direct answers despite independent contexts and chronology.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q17/p1", "position": "One passage can clarify another, as this denial answers the accusation elsewhere.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, cited through Ibn Hishām, says the Qur'an is like one sūra and pairs 15:6 with 68:2. {"id": "68:2/q18", "question": "What supporting disciplines and reports does Ibn ʿĀshūr associate with interpreting such passages?", "turns_on": "The disagreement concerns whether a discipline is a prerequisite source of tafsīr or merely aids fuller argument.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q18/p1", "position": "Uṣūl al-fiqh supplies language methods and organized rules for deriving legal meanings.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it explains implication, contrary implication and other methods grammarians omit; al-Ghazālī counts it among Qur'anic and legal sciences. He says it also systematizes inference from commands, prohibitions and general wording."}, {"id": "68:2/q18/p2", "position": "Kalām is a prerequisite because one must establish that God speaks or know what can be ascribed to Him.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm gives the first reason; al-Ālūsī, deriving from al-Jurjānī, gives the second and cites 20:5. Ibn ʿĀshūr finds al-Ālūsī's rationale closer but rejects both as requirements for tafsīr: God speaking was established before kalām, and extended argument does not make a discipline a source of exegesis."}, {"id": "68:2/q18/p3", "position": "Fiqh can enrich exegesis but is derived from it and is not a prerequisite source.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects al-Suyūṭī's inclusion of fiqh as a tafsīr source; it helps elaborate legal meanings, etiquette and inference. {"id": "68:2/q19", "question": "How does the later phrase about al-maftūn describe who is mad?", "turns_on": "Whether al-maftūn names an affliction, an afflicted person, or a group containing the madman.", "positions": [{"id": "68:2/q19/p1", "position": "Al-maftūn is a verbal noun meaning trial or temptation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī compares maʿqūl and maḥṣūl used for a thing's rationality or outcome."}, {"id": "68:2/q19/p2", "position": "Al-maftūn is a passive participle, 'the afflicted one,' with an extra bāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports that the clause depends on 'they will see.'"}, {"id": "68:2/q19/p3", "position": "The bāʾ means 'in': which of the Muslims or disbelievers contains the madman.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Farrāʾ and cites a rajaz line using an extra bāʾ in 'we hope for relief.'"}]}

{"id": "68:4/q02", "question": "What does ʿalā convey in the phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿalā is read as possession and establishment or as mastery.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q02/p1", "position": "It presents great character as something firmly possessed and inhabited by the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī takes ʿalā as possession or inherence and compares 39:22. {"id": "68:4/q03", "question": "What does khuluq mean and how is it distinguished from related words?", "turns_on": "The extent of the word's semantic field and how its cognates differ.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q03/p1", "position": "It is a settled inward disposition or cultivated manner from which conduct flows readily.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and Ibn al-Jawzī contrast cultivated khuluq with innate khaym; al-Aʿshā's poem illustrates khaym. Rāzī stresses effortless action versus the act itself. Al-Rāghib and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrast inward khuluq with visible khalq; Asad includes habitual conduct that becomes second nature. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾ note unqualified khuluq usually means good character. Elmalılı gives its plurals huluk and akhlāq and Turkish usage."}, {"id": "68:4/q03/p2", "position": "Its cognate khalāq denotes an allotted share, particularly otherworldly recompense.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ records al-Farrāʾ on 2:102, Abū ʿUbayda on 3:77, al-Rāghib's narrower earned-virtue sense, and al-Ṭabarī's transmitted share glosses including Ibn ʿAbbās's 'what sustains him.' She prefers share, citing a Prophetic saying, and compares 40:47, 42:20 and 4:7. She also distinguishes ikhtilāq, invention or fabricated speech."}, {"id": "68:4/q03/p3", "position": "Khuluq can include a settled readiness for true knowledge as well as practical conduct.", "reasons": "Rāzī replies to his own theoretical-versus-practical distinction: habit can concern cognition or action, and a soul can be effortlessly receptive to true knowledge and unreceptive to false belief."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q04", "question": "How is the greatness of the character expressed?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective heightens human character or alludes to divine attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q04/p1", "position": "ʿAẓīm marks exceptional excellence and rank; the indefinite khuluq magnifies a quality beyond full human comprehension.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī glosses ʿaẓīm as excellent or good. {"id": "68:4/q05", "question": "What is the Prophet's great character?", "turns_on": "The sources variously identify character with Islam, Qur'anic conduct, human virtues, social conduct, or inward states; objections concern lexical usage, chronology, context and the scope of the praise.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q05/p1", "position": "It is the Qur'an embodied as manners, obedience, and avoidance of its prohibitions.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha repeatedly calls his character the Qur'an, sometimes reciting 23:1–10; ʿAlī, ʿAṭiyya and al-Ḥasan call it Qur'anic discipline. Qatāda specifies commands and prohibitions; 7:199 and 16:90 supply examples. Al-Qurṭubī prefers ʿĀʾisha's Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim report; al-Zajjāj prefers divinely commanded Qur'anic conduct. Ibn Kathīr adds God-given virtues; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı explain that he embodied all virtues and rejected defects, with 11:112. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes the early Meccan chronology objection. Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and Asad list transmission routes."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p2", "position": "It is the great religion of Islam, or the divinely entrusted way of life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others give this gloss; some call Islam God's dearest and most pleasing religion. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk includes the entire entrusted command. Al-Naḥḥās expands it to doctrine, way and obedience; Asad prefers 'way of life' from dīn. Rāzī objects that religion chiefly perfects knowledge whereas character perfects action; Ṭabāṭabāʾ accepts the reports only insofar as Islam includes contextual social virtue; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the Qur'an nowhere uses khuluq for religion."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p3", "position": "It is the highest noble human disposition, gathering every virtue.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī prefers the apparent sense. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī cite his mission to perfect noble traits. Al-Jubbāʾī lists patience, generosity, judgment, endurance, pardon and freedom from envy. Ibn ʿĀshūr enumerates piety, knowledge, justice, humility, chastity, courage and more; Rāzī distinguishes practical perfection from knowledge at 4:113 and says 6:90 gathered the earlier prophets' diverse virtues in him. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ grounds the praise in virtues known since youth."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p4", "position": "It is exceptional patience, gentleness, forgiveness and generosity in dealing with people.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī stress bearing abuse; al-Ālūsī says he bore more than other resolute prophets. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ lists steadfastness, tact and humility as the context's social virtues; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī mention honoring the community. Rāzī details gracious speech and lenience, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya names justice, pardon and maintaining ties."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p5", "position": "He outwardly lives with people while his inward attention remains fixed on God.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī repeats this and a sage counsels sincerity with God alongside truth with people; al-Junayd and al-Ṭabrisī give the same outward/inward distinction."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p6", "position": "His only aspiration is God, so created things and people's harshness do not capture his heart.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd names sole aspiration; al-Wāsiṭī says he neither disputes nor is drawn into dispute after Night Journey knowledge. Al-Ḥusayn says beholding the Real makes harshness ineffective and creation small; al-Qāsim says the cosmos leaves no effect. Abū Saʿīd says no concern remains apart from God."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p7", "position": "He relinquished both this world and the next for the Real.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ give the exchange; al-Nasafī says he was generous with both worlds and relied upon their Creator; al-Qushayrī reports the refusal of earthly keys and the Night Journey vision without looking away, citing 53:17."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p8", "position": "He embodies divine attributes and is sustained by God rather than his own strength.", "reasons": "Sahl traces mercy to abandoning reliance on personal power and cites God's patient self-description to David; al-Wāsiṭī places Muhammad's manifestation of divine qualities beside Jesus, Āṣif and Moses' staff, while insisting they belong to God. Abū Saʿīd names generosity, forbearance and forgiveness and cites the report about more than one hundred traits. Al-Qāshānī cites 16:127; al-Murṣafī reads ʿĀʾisha this way."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p9", "position": "His self-will and independent choice disappear in submission to divine decree.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī calls abandonment of will his greatest character; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ adds surrender to decree and forgiveness and annihilation of self and attachments."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p10", "position": "He sees through God's witnessing and enjoys divine disclosure in his inner secret.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn contrasts divine witnessing with ruinous self-seeing; al-Wāsiṭī speaks of the sweetness of beholding and lights adorning the secret, with a third direct communion favoring him above creation."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p11", "position": "His character marks movement beyond moral attributes into annihilation and abiding in the divine Essence.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn says he reached the Essence's reality and that passing beyond annihilation is followed by abiding."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p12", "position": "He devoted himself wholly, then was veiled after presence.", "reasons": "Fāris gives this sequence as the state of a person of great character."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p13", "position": "Its exaltation contains treasures of provision.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh gives this inward explanation."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p14", "position": "It is the essence of faith and the reality of divine oneness.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar gives this inward gloss."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p15", "position": "It was refined through estrangement, hardship and withdrawal from pleasures.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says God placed him in the Hijaz and exposed him to hardship until moral blemishes were removed, then called his character great."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p16", "position": "It is a soul naturally drawn to the unseen and away from bodily and worldly pleasures.", "reasons": "Rāzī draws this reading from ʿĀʾisha's Qur'an description."}, {"id": "68:4/q05/p17", "position": "It is exceptionally high because God granted him favors beyond those of other prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī places the fashioning of this character after surpassing grants of divine favor."}]}

The versions are transmitted by al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Ṭabāṭabāʾ, Kur'an Yolu and Study Quran; al-Baghawī states no grade and Ibn Kathīr notes Aḥmad's unique route."}, {"id": "68:4/q06/p4", "position": "His character was known even before revelation through trustworthiness, truth and service.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites Abū Ṭālib's marriage speech, Khadīja's list of kinship, truth, trust, hospitality and help, and Quraysh's title 'the trustworthy.'"}]}
{"id": "68:4/q07", "question": "What occasion is reported for the verse's revelation?", "turns_on": "The reported occasions identify different episodes and scopes of the passage.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q07/p1", "position": "His gracious response to anyone who summoned him occasioned the verse.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha says no one had better character: to family and companions alike he answered 'at your service.' Al-Wāḥidī, al-Suyūṭī and al-Durr transmit the occasion."}, {"id": "68:4/q07/p2", "position": "A report locates the surrounding polemic in insults to ʿAlī after the Prophet honored him.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says Quraysh's slander of ʿAlī explains the passage's contrast of those astray and guided."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q08", "question": "What does good character comprise and require?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize practical social virtues or an inward spiritual transformation.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q08/p1", "position": "It joins devotion to God with just, generous and gentle treatment of people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya names justice, beneficence, pardon and ties; Ibn al-Mubārak names a pleasant face, doing good and avoiding harm. Biqāʿī divides duties toward God, rulings and people, and links Islam especially to modesty; a report calls modesty its defining character. The Prophet's instruction to Abū Dharr joins reverence, repairing bad deeds and good treatment; Rāzī details generosity, speech, restraint of anger and lenient dealings."}, {"id": "68:4/q08/p2", "position": "The greatest spiritual gift is changing a blameworthy trait into a praiseworthy one.", "reasons": "Sahl says other marvels soon pass, while character transformation endures; al-Muntakhab likewise describes divine favor removing blame and supplying praise."}, {"id": "68:4/q08/p3", "position": "It is the greatest spiritual station because it connects one to divine attributes.", "reasons": "Sahl and al-Wāsiṭī distinguish this connection from lower stations tied to ordinary people, citing God's patience and His command to David to take on His qualities."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q09", "question": "What rewards or standing do reports attach to good character?", "turns_on": "The reports name distinct rewards and rankings; some combine them in a single narration.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q09/p1", "position": "It brings Paradise, while bad character or misuse of the mouth and sexual organ brings the Fire.", "reasons": "ʿAlī's report and the report through al-Riḍā contrast Paradise and Fire. In Abū Hurayra's report, God-consciousness and good character chiefly admit to Paradise, while mouth and sexual organ lead to Hell; al-Tirmidhī calls the latter ṣaḥīḥ gharīb. Study Quran repeats the Paradise point."}, {"id": "68:4/q09/p2", "position": "It weighs especially heavily in the judgment balance.", "reasons": "Abū al-Dardāʾ's report is repeated by al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī. Al-Qurṭubī gives one route graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ, adding that God hates obscene speech, and another called gharīb."}, {"id": "68:4/q09/p3", "position": "It raises its possessor to the rank of one who prays by night and fasts by day.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha's and later Prophetic reports give the comparison; al-Qurṭubī's combined balance-and-rank route is called gharīb by al-Tirmidhī."}, {"id": "68:4/q09/p4", "position": "Those of finest character are especially loved and near to God or the Prophet; gossips and arrogant speakers are far.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's reports oppose easy, loving people to divisive tale-bearers. Jābir's report places the best-mannered nearest the Prophet on Judgment Day and affected arrogant speakers farthest; al-Tirmidhī calls it ḥasan gharīb, and explains mutafayhiqūn as arrogant with an Abū Hurayra parallel. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Study Quran transmit best-character sayings."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q10", "question": "How does this praise relate to the surrounding denial of madness and the sūra?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the praise to refutation, consolation, the opening Pen, or the wider moral contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q10/p1", "position": "The character praise refutes the charge of madness and strengthens the Prophet under deniers' abuse.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the opening answers charges of poetry, magic and madness and follows a prior contrast of blessed and wretched; the reward promise and this praise encourage patience. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds keen understanding and good temperament. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees renewed refutation with matching emphases; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ sees early reassurance and a closing echo at 68:51. Iṣlāḥī contrasts the Prophet's morals with poets and soothsayers; Kur'an Yolu calls him a trustworthy model. Some, reported by al-Ālūsī, argue good morals and madness cannot coexist."}, {"id": "68:4/q10/p2", "position": "The ordering and wording protect and honor the Prophet before quoting his accusers.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says denial precedes the accusation and character praise comes before its quotation at 68:51 to soften the impact; he also contrasts the Prophet's reason with his opponents' lack of it after 68:3. Al-Wāḥidī sees praise joined to a reward promise."}, {"id": "68:4/q10/p3", "position": "The verse is a supreme sign in the Pen's written testimony to revelation and character.", "reasons": "Elmalılı links it to 68:1, prefers the primordial or Highest Pen because Muhammad did not read or write before revelation (29:48; 42:52), and reads reward and moral contrast as clarifying the Pen's significance."}, {"id": "68:4/q10/p4", "position": "The sūra's account of social vice contrasts with this character.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says al-Qalam's hammaz and list of bad traits with a command not to obey fit its social-conduct focus; unlike al-Humaza, it gives little detail about the final outcome."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q11", "question": "Why are the Qur'anic words fitting to this praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q11/p1", "position": "Divine knowledge supplies precisely fitting words and meanings, making the Qur'an maximally eloquent.", "reasons": "Al-Bārizī says humans cannot reliably summon each meaning with its best expression, whereas God knows both; his general principle explains the Qur'an's eloquence."}, {"id": "68:4/q11/p2", "position": "The verse stacks emphatic devices as assurance and as reinforcement of the preceding oath response.", "reasons": "Elmalılı counts inna, lām, magnifying tanwīn and ʿaẓīm, tied to 68:1–2."}]}
{"id": "68:4/q12", "question": "What further testimony illustrates the praise of his character?", "turns_on": "The transmitted illustrations invoke testimony, prayer, obedience, or perception.", "positions": [{"id": "68:4/q12/p1", "position": "ʿĀʾisha testified that he was the best of people in character and that his character was the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits both parts of her testimony."}, {"id": "68:4/q12/p2", "position": "The Prophet prayed for beautiful character corresponding to the beautiful form God gave him.", "reasons": "Study Quran transmits the prayer as an analogy between inward character and outward form."}, {"id": "68:4/q12/p3", "position": "His character fulfilled God's command to take the forgiving course.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī cites 7:199 as the divine instruction he carried out."}, {"id": "68:4/q12/p4", "position": "God made created colors small in his sight so he could know their Creator.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports this as an explanation of how God magnified his character."}]}
